test_title: PYST 61: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 24 Dec, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Which of the following best describes a person with hypermetropia?

options.text: They are unable to see anything without glasses
Their vision is equally blurred for both near and distant objects
They can see nearby objects clearly but distant ones appear blurry
They can see faraway objects clearly but struggle to see things up close

solution:
The correct answer is __**They can see faraway objects clearly but struggle to see things up close**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hypermetropia**, also commonly known as **farsightedness**, is a vision condition where a person can see distant objects clearly, but objects nearby appear blurry. ***Hence, the correct answer is option 4.***
 
• In a hypermetropic eye, the light rays coming from a nearby object are not focused on the **retina** but instead converge at a point **behind the retina**. This results in a blurred image for close-up tasks like reading or sewing.
 
• This defect arises because either the **focal length** of the eye lens is too long or the **eyeball** has become too **short**. Because the eye cannot increase its converging power sufficiently, the **near point** of the person moves farther away than the standard **25 cm**.
 
• To correct this vision defect, a **convex lens** (converging lens) of appropriate power is used. The lens provides the additional focusing power required to bring the light rays together exactly on the **retina**.
 
• A person with **hypermetropia** often experiences **eye strain** or headaches after performing close-work activities for a long duration due to the constant effort of the **ciliary muscles** to focus.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Myopia (Nearsightedness):**
 
 
• This is the opposite of hypermetropia, where a person can see nearby objects clearly but distant objects appear blurry.
 
• The image is formed **in front of the retina** rather than on it, often due to an **elongated eyeball** or excessive curvature of the lens.
 
• It is corrected using a **concave lens** (diverging lens), which diverges the light rays before they enter the eye, allowing them to focus correctly on the **retina**.
 
 
 
• **Presbyopia:**
 
 
• This condition is associated with **aging**, usually occurring after the age of **40**. It is caused by the gradual weakening of the **ciliary muscles** and the diminishing flexibility of the **crystalline lens**.
 
• The person finds it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably without corrective glasses, similar to hypermetropia, but the underlying cause is **loss of accommodation**.
 
• It is often corrected using **bifocal lenses**, where the upper portion is concave for distant vision and the lower portion is convex for reading.
 
 
 
• **Astigmatism:**
 
 
• This occurs when the **cornea** or the lens is not perfectly spherical, having different curvatures in different planes.
 
• As a result, light rays do not focus on a single point on the **retina**, causing vision to be blurred or distorted at all distances. It is typically corrected using **cylindrical lenses**.
 
 
 
• **Cataract:**
 
 
• This is a medical condition where the lens of the eye becomes **cloudy** or opaque, leading to a progressive loss of vision.
 
• It is most common in **older adults** and is treated through a surgical procedure where the cloudy lens is replaced with an artificial **intraocular lens (IOL)**.
 
 
 
• **Optical Power:**
 
 
• The power of a corrective lens is measured in **Dioptres (D)**. For **Hypermetropia**, the prescription power is **positive (+)**, whereas for **Myopia**, it is **negative (-)**.
